steps.observation: Work on this for 30 seconds; do not stop early. Write a short story about a lighthouse keeper.

steps.action:
The storms had been getting stranger.

Elias noticed it first in the way the light behaved. On clear nights his lamp at Graymarsh Point threw a clean, steady beam that swept the rocks in a perfect rhythm: twelve seconds dark, three seconds bright, twelve seconds dark. He had watched it for twenty-three years, had set his sleep and meals and memories to that turning.

But in the last month, whenever clouds rolled in from the horizon, the beam seemed to thicken, as if traveling through something heavier than air. The glass lens was spotless, the lamp itself sound. Yet the light bent wrong, curving toward the sea in a soft, sorrowful arc.

He mentioned it to no one, because there was no one to mention it to. The mainland village had emptied out two winters ago when the fish stopped coming and the cannery closed. Supply boats still arrived every second Tuesday—weather permitting—and a young man from the Harbor Office would leave crates of food and kerosene at the end of the broken pier, wave once, and turn his engine back toward the living world.

Elias liked the isolation. Or told himself he did. The lighthouse had its own voice: the slow tick of the clockwork that turned the lamp, the low moan of wind in the railing, the distant percussion of waves meeting rock. He moved through its spiral stairs and narrow rooms like a ghost who had decided to haunt only one place and do it properly.

The night the ship came, the rain was so hard it felt like a second sea falling from the sky.

He woke to the first distant boom of thunder and climbed to the lantern room, lantern in hand, his joints complaining. Lightning flickered at the edges of the world, outlining a jagged line of cloud. He checked the lamp—flame steady, glass clean, mechanism winding smooth. Outside, the air tasted metallic.

Then he saw a light where no light should be.

Far out, beyond the safest channels and directly over the hidden reef, a pale gleam bobbed in the dark. Not the clean line of another vessel’s lamp: something lower, weaker, like a candle being carried through a gale.

Elias reached for the brass spyglass hanging from its hook and aimed into the storm. The rain blurred everything, but between sheets of water he caught a shape: a small vessel, too close to the teeth of rock, its mast already shivering under the assault.

He knew that stretch of sea intimately. On calm days he had watched seals sunning themselves on the black stone, and on harsh days had watched the waves explode into fans of white that reached twenty feet into the air. The ship was in the wrong place entirely. Any seasoned captain would have kept well clear.

“See me,” he whispered, turning his lamp by hand to sweep the beam more insistently across the danger. “Turn. See me.”

The beam cut through the rain, then faltered. For a moment the light smeared sideways, bending toward the small vessel as if it were being drawn there. Elias blinked, wiped the inside of the glass again, checked the flame. Perfect.

The storm roared in closer, and with it came a sound that did not belong: a faint, chiming note that seemed to ring inside his teeth.

On the sea, the pale gleam of the ship flickered. The spyglass showed shadows rushing over its deck, lines snapping loose, a figure at the wheel fighting the wind. No one was looking toward the lighthouse.

Elias had guided countless ships through fog and gale, and in all those years there had always been that answering flick of acknowledgement: a signal lamp swinging in response, a horn blast, even a single raised arm when a deckhand happened to be looking his way. This captain did not see him. The vessel plowed straight toward the reef.

Heart hammering, he did the only thing he could: he took the light.

He had never extinguished it in a storm. The manual said never to, the law said never to, the man who had trained him had looked him in the eye and said, “This flame is your oath, Elias. You keep it burning.”

But the beam was not doing what it was supposed to do. And the strange chiming in the air was growing louder, syncing with the rhythm of his turning lamp.

“Forgive me,” he muttered to no one, and closed the flame.

Darkness crashed in around the tower. The lighthouse, emptied of its beacon, felt suddenly like a hollow bone. Elias worked by instinct, his hands going to the old emergency kit beneath the bench: flares, an oilskin coat, the heavy steel signal lantern no one used anymore.

He lit the lantern. Its small, stubborn flame glowed yellow and imperfect. Cradling it under his coat, he descended the spiral stairs, feeling his way down by memory as much as touch. The wind forced the thick wooden door open like a hand from outside.

Rain hit him sideways. The path to the cliff edge had long since lost its railing, so Elias moved carefully, boots slick on moss and old salt. The sea was a white madness below. He could no longer see the ship at all.

He lifted the lantern as high as he could and began to swing it back and forth: a crude imitation of the great lens above, a man’s small arm trying to match the sweep of the earth’s turning.

“Here!” he shouted, though his voice went nowhere in that noise. “Here, turn!”

For a long, terrifying moment, there was nothing but storm.

Then, through a tear in the rain, he saw it: the pale gleam again, far too close to the reef. But now the chiming sound spiked, sharp as shattered glass, and the little vessel’s light jerked—no, jumped—sideways, as if something had yanked it.

Elias saw, with a clarity that would wake him for the rest of his life, that it was not moving across the water so much as sliding along a line in the air. The glow slewed away from the reef, arcing toward his feeble swinging lamp.

His arm ached. He kept swinging.

The strange bending of the lighthouse’s great beam, the thickened air, the chiming that bit at his bones—whatever had warped the night’s light seemed to be clawing for this ship, or for any light at all. Without meaning to, something had gone wrong with his own beacon: it had curved toward the peril instead of away from it.

But this small lantern was different. Its flame shook and spat, irregular as a heartbeat. It did not offer the clean, sure promise of the tower’s lamp. It wavered, human and fallible.

The pale vessel’s glow jerked again and this time held its new course.

Minutes or hours later—time had no meaning in the blitz of rain and adrenaline—the churning water smoothed a fraction, and the sound of waves changed pitch. The reef lay behind that ship now. It would live, if its hull had not already been torn.

Elias kept swinging the lantern until his shoulder gave out and the flame finally sighed into darkness, drowned by an especially vicious gust.

He stood alone above the sea, arm throbbing, soaked through to the marrow. The chiming in the air faded with the retreating storm.

Slowly, he climbed back into the tower.

He relit the main lamp with fingers that would not stop shaking. The great lens caught the new flame and threw it into its old, familiar arc: twelve seconds dark, three seconds bright, perfect and straight. No bending. No thickness. As if nothing had happened.

Exhausted, he slumped onto the narrow bench and stared at the glass, waiting for some sign that the world had tilted permanently. The night gave him only the soft hiss of rain easing off the pane.

In the morning, the sky was scrubbed clean and blue as enamel. Sea birds wheeled and argued. On the horizon, a small, distant smudge of sail moved away, already forgetting the shore.

No report came. No letter from the Harbor Office, no curious young man asking why the light at Graymarsh Point had gone dark at the height of a storm. Perhaps the ship had been too far to see his tower after all. Perhaps no one had recorded the anomaly of bent light and broken rhythm.

Elias went back to his rounds: oiling the gears, checking the wick, polishing the lens until he could see his own tired face multiplied in its facets.

At night, when the wind was up and the sea began its low chants, he sometimes heard again that faint chiming note. The beam would pass cleanly across the water, but he would step closer to the glass, watching for any hint of curve.

On a clear evening some weeks later, a supply boat docked and the young man from the Harbor Office bounded up the path with a folded newspaper under his arm.

“Thought you might like to see this,” he said, grinning in the doorway. “Miracle out on the reef. Or near it, anyway.”

Elias took the paper. On the front of the local section was a small photograph of a familiar stretch of coastline, the reef beneath Graymarsh labeled in cramped print. The headline read: COASTAL SCHOONER SAVED IN FREAK STORM—CAPTAIN REPORTS ‘LIGHT MOVED ITSELF.’

He read the captain’s account twice. The man described a strange, bell-like sound before his instruments failed, his compass spinning. His own running lights had flared too bright, painting the deck in ghostly white. “Then,” the quote said, “I swear the sea lit up like glass, and some kind of glow grabbed us sideways. I thought we were done for. But something else—something dimmer, more like a lantern—swung out of nowhere and we just… slid. Like a hand took hold and pulled us off the rocks.”

No one, the article concluded with a journalist’s shrug, had reported unusual activity from the lighthouse at Graymarsh Point. The Harbor Office confirmed that its logs showed the beacon functioning normally throughout the night.

“Anyway.” The young man scratched his head. “Makes for a good story. People like miracles.”

Elias folded the paper carefully and set it on the shelf above the oil tins.

“People like explanations,” he said.

The young man laughed and went back down to his boat, whistling.

That night, Elias trimmed the wick with particular care. When he lit the lamp, he waited, watching the flame cling, then steady. The great lens took hold of it and sent it on its measured way, reliable as breath.

He stood there a long while, listening to the quiet tick of the turning gears.

The storms were getting stranger. The world seemed to be learning new ways to misbehave. But his duty had not changed: to keep a light burning, not as a perfect answer, but as an honest one. A human-made flame, stubborn in the dark.

If the night bent and the sea sang and the air itself shifted, he would be ready, lantern in hand, to step outside when the great, flawless beam wasn’t enough.

Somewhere beyond the horizon, a captain told a story in harbor taverns about a crooked little light that had saved him when the big one failed.

Up on Graymarsh Point, the lighthouse keeper stayed at his post, listening for the first distant thunder, feeling for the first, almost-imperceptible warp in the way the night received his light.
